title: Real-world prognostic factors for first-line EGFR-TKI efficacy in advanced NSCLC patients harboring EGFR 21 L858R mutation
author: Yan’e Liu; Lu Chen; Xin Zhu; Hua Zhang; Baoshan Cao
text:
Abstract
Objective
This study aimed to investigate the prognostic factors for the treatment efficacy of epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation.
Methods
The study enrolled patients with advanced EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC who received first-line EGFR-TKI treatment between January 2019 and April 2024. Cox regression analyses were performed to identify the prognostic factors from clinical characteristics and concomitant genetic alterations that influenced progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS).
Results
According to the study of a cohort of 120 patients, we found that more metastatic organs (≥3 organs), specific metastatic patterns (liver and bone involvement), concurrent TP53 mutations, and worse Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS) were associated with shorter PFS. And ECOG PS was an independent predictive factor for PFS. Similarly, metastatic organs ≥ 3 (HR, 2.719; 95 % CI, 1.386–5.333; p = 0.004), ECOG PS of 2 (HR, 10.756; 95 % CI, 4.002–28.906; p < 0.001), and body mass index (BMI)＞24 kg/m2 (HR, 0.335; 95 % CI, 0.147–0.760; p = 0.009) were associated with worse OS. We also observed that patients harboring TP53 co-mutations demonstrated significantly inferior PFS compared with their TP53 wild-type counterparts (13.7 months vs. 18.8 months; p = 0.006).
Conclusions
This study identified several factors significantly associated with worse response to EGFR-TKIs in NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R mutation and respective independent predictive factors for PFS and OS. These findings could enable personalized therapeutic efficacy assessment to facilitate clinical decision-making for EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC patients treated with EGFR-TKIs.
Keywords: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), EGFR Exon 21 L858R mutation, Targeted therapy, TP53
Introduction
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations are the most frequent genetic alterations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), accounting for approximately 55.9% of patients in China [1]. Within this population, the EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation has been reported as one of the most common variants, observed in around 28.1% of NSCLC patients [1].
EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) are the first-line treatment for advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients [2], [3]. Despite the remarkable clinical efficacy of EGFR-TKIs, treatment outcomes can vary substantially: while some patients experience prolonged benefits over several years, others show rapid disease progression within weeks. Resistance inevitably emerges in patients treated with EGFR-TKIs, often requiring alternative therapeutic strategies. Lower resistance rates were reported in third-generation EGFR-TKIs treatment, reaching approximately 20%–30% [4]. These variations in treatment response are largely attributable to the types of EGFR mutations. Among them, preferable responses have been observed in NSCLC patients with EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation and exon 19 deletions (19del), while the former showed relatively reduced responsiveness to EGFR-TKIs therapy [5], [6]. Therefore, better prognostic predictions for each mutation subtype could benefit the clinical practice. However, the specific prognostic factors for EGFR L858R-mutant patients remain unclear.
Previous studies showed that Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS), co-mutations, and metastatic burden were associated with survival outcomes of patients with EGFR-sensitizing mutation [7], [8]. However, it is not yet known whether baseline characteristics are also related to EGFR-TKI treatment responses as prediction factors. In addition, co-mutations with EGFR have also been intensively studied for their distinctive effects on EGFR-TKI treatments, such as TP53 and KRAS [9], [10], [11], [12]. And co-mutations have been increasingly recognized as potential negative prognostic indicators in EGFR-mutant NSCLC [13], [14]. Recent evidence has highlighted that EGFR exon 21-mutant tumors are more likely to harbor concomitant genetic alterations, which may negatively impact patient prognosis [15], [16]. The occurrent mutations in patients with EGFR L858R mutant could also contribute to the precise of prognostic prediction.
In this study, we comprehensively analyzed survival outcomes data, clinicopathological characteristics, and molecular profiling of NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R mutation. We identified several prognostic factors associated with clinical outcomes in NSCLC patients harboring the EGFRL858R mutation, including extensive metastatic burden, concurrent TP53 mutations, worse ECOG PS, and reduced body mass index (BMI). Therefore, these findings provide valuable insights into the risk stratification and management of EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC.
Methods
Participants
Advanced NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R mutation were consecutively enrolled between January 2019 and April 2024 at the Peking University Third Hospital. The inclusion criteria were as follows: 1) aged 18 years and older; 2) pathologically confirmed NSCLC including lung adenocarcinoma, squamous carcinoma, or other non-specific pathologic types; 3) patients with stage IIIB, IIIC, or IV according to the TNM staging system of the American Joint Committee on Cancer eighth edition; 4) EGFR L858R mutation detected by next-generation sequencing (NGS) of baseline tissue specimens before treatment; 5) treated with EGFR-TKIs at the first-line therapy; and 6) complete radiological efficacy evaluation conducted at 2–3 month intervals and follow-up records. The exclusion criteria were as follows: 1) unavailable original genetic testing report; 2) first-line treatment without EGFR-TKIs; 3) incomplete disease staging information; and 4) incomplete radiological efficacy evaluation or follow-up data.
Data collection and treatment assessment
Comprehensive clinical data were systematically extracted from the Hospital Information System (HIS), including demographic characteristics (age, sex, height, and weight), smoking status, comorbidities (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary heart disease, and diabetes mellitus), ECOG PS, pathological features, baseline stage, sites of metastasis, NGS genetic profiling, and first-line EGFR-TKI treatment details (including TKI types, initiation dates, and disease progression time).
Tumor response was evaluated through serial radiological assessments conducted at 2–3 month intervals. Ttreatment assessment followed the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1 guidelines [17]. Treatment responses were categorized as follows: complete response (CR), partial response (PR), stable disease (SD), and progressive disease (PD) for measurable lesions; CR, PD, and non-CR/non-PD for non-measurable lesions. Overall response rate (ORR) was defined as the proportion of patients who achieved CR or PR. Disease Control Rate (DCR) was calculated as the percentage of patients achieving CR, PR, or SD. PFS was calculated from the commencement of TKI therapy until disease progression or death from any cause. OS was defined as the duration from treatment initiation to mortality from all causes.
Genetic testing methods
As a retrospective study, NGS-based genetic profiling of each participant was obtained. A subset 45 patients underwent a 196 or 425 cancer-related genes pan-cancer panel performed on DNBSEQ-T7 platform, and the rest 75 patients were subjected to a 26 lung-cancer-related gene panel testing using the Ion Torrent Proton high-throughput sequencing platform. This study focused on detecting mutations, short insertions/deletions, and fusion variants in 26 lung cancer-related genes, including EGFR, ALK, BRAF, TP53, ERBB2, ERBB4, KRAS, MAP2K1, MET, NRAS, PIK3CA, RET, ROS1, AKT1, CTNNB1, DDR2, FBXW7, FGFR1, FGFR2, FGFR3, NOTCH1, NTRK1, PTEN, SMAD4, STK11, and UGT1A1.
Statistical analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 26.0 and R software version 4.2.0. Continuous variables were compared between groups using the Wilcoxon test, while categorical variables were analyzed using Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact test, as appropriate. Survival analyses were performed using the Kaplan-Meier method, with between-group comparisons assessed by the log-rank test. Both univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression models were employed to identify independent prognostic factors among demographic, clinical, and genomic characteristics. P values less than 0.05 were considered as statistically significant.
Results
Clinical characteristics of 120 patients
The study cohort consisted of 120 treatment-naïve advanced NSCLC patients with EGFRL858R mutations (Fig. 1). Demographic analysis revealed a median age of 66 years (range: 41–92), with a female predominance (81/120, 67.5%). Adenocarcinoma was diagnosed in the majority of patients, accounting for 95% of the cases (114/120). At initial diagnosis, 91.7% of patients (110/120) presented with stage IV, while 23.3% (28/120) exhibited metastases in more than three organs. At the first-line treatment, 55.0% (66/120) of patients received first-generation TKIs (gefitinib/icotinib/erlotinib), 18.3% (22/120) with second-generation (afatinib/dacomitinib), and 26.7% (32/120) with third-generation (osimertinib/almonertinib) (Table 1).

Frequency of EGFR concurrent mutations
We analyzed the genomic profiling of all 120 NSCLC patients using pretreatment tissue samples, focused on 26 lung cancer-related genes. In this EGFR L858R-mutant cohort, we identified several coexisting genetic alterations, which were categorized into two distinct groups: (1) tumor suppressor gene alterations, predominantly featuring TP53 mutations (40.8%, 49/120), with additional PTEN aberrations observed in 1.7% (2/120) of cases; and (2) concurrent driver mutations, including MET amplifications (3.3%, 4/120), ERBB2 amplifications (1.7%, 2/120), KRAS mutations (1.7%, 2/120), BRAF mutations (0.8%, 1/120), RET fusions (1.7%, 2/120), ALK mutations (0.8%, 1/120), EGFR L861Q mutations (0.8%, 1/120), and EGFR S768I mutations (0.8%, 1/120). These genomic alterations are visually summarized in Fig. 2.
Clinical outcomes of 120 NSCLC patients treated with first-line EGFR-TKIs
The follow-up period was extended until November 30, 2024, with a median follow-up duration of 41.2 months. Disease progression had occurred in 73.3% of patients (88/120), while 35.8% (43/120) had succumbed to the disease.
The study population demonstrated a DCR of 95.8% (115/120), and an ORR of 58.3% (70/120), with a median PFS (mPFS) of 16.5 months (95%CI, 13.8–19.1). Tumor burden (defined by the number of metastatic organs) significantly affected PFS. Patients with metastases in ≥ 3 organs had a 1.688-fold increased risk of progression compared with those with 0–2 organs (95% CI, 1.033–2.759, p = 0.034) (Fig. 3a). Site-specific analysis revealed significantly shorter PFS in patients with liver (p = 0.020) or bone metastases (p = 0.043) compared with those without these two metastatic sites (Table 2). Molecular characterization identified TP53 mutation as a risk factor for disease progression, as patients with mutated TP53 exhibiting a 1.821-fold higher risk of progression than wild-type counterparts (95% CI: 1.184–2.801; p = 0.006) (Fig. 3b). In addition, patients with ECOG PS of 2 had significantly reduced PFS than those with ECOG PS of 0–1 (Fig. 3c). Multivariate Cox regression analysis identified that ECOG PS of 2 was the sole independent predictive factor for PFS (HR, 2.904; 95% CI: 1.269–6.642 (Table 2).

The median OS (mOS) for all 120 patients was not reached. Univariate Cox regression analysis identified that metastatic organs ≥ 3 (p = 0.001), ECOG PS of 2 (p < 0.001), and BMI > 24 kg/m2 (p = 0.013) were significantly associated with OS (Table 3). Multivariate analysis further confirmed that these three parameters were independent risk factors for OS, that is, metastatic organs ≥ 3 (HR, 2.719; 95%CI, 1.386–5.333; p = 0.004), ECOG PS= 2 (HR, 10.756; 95% CI, 4.002–28.906; p < 0.001), and BMI＞24 kg/m2 (HR, 0.335; 95% CI, 0.147–0.760, P = 0.009) (Table 3). Notably, TP53 mutation status did not demonstrate a significant association with OS (Table 3). The KM survival curves for PFS, stratified by respective factors, were consistent with these findings (Fig. 4a-d).

Patients receiving first-line treatment with either first-, second-, or third-generation EGFR-TKIs showed comparable ORR (57.6% [38/66], 54.5% [12/22], and 62.5% [20/32], p = 0.829). No statistically significant differences were observed in PFS or OS among these three treatment groups (Table 2, Table 3).
Clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes of patients with or without TP53 mutation
The prevalence of EGFR L858R and TP53 co-mutation in our NSCLC cohort was 40.8% (49/120). Comparative analyses of baseline characteristics between patients with mutated (N = 49) and wild-type (N = 71) TP53 are summarized in Table 4. Notably, patients with concurrent TP53 mutation had significantly heavier tumor burden, as evidenced by a higher proportion of cases with no less than 3 metastatic organs than these with wild-type TP53 (32.7% [16/49] vs. 16.9% [12/71], p = 0.045). Furthermore, TP53-mutant patients demonstrated significantly higher incidence rates of liver metastasis (16.3% [8/49] vs. 4.2% [3/71], p = 0.024) and bone metastasis (59.2% [29/49] vs. 40.8% [29/71], p = 0.036). However, no significant differences were observed in sex, age, smoking status, BMI, comorbidities, pathological features, other metastatic organs (excluding liver and bone), or EGFR-TKI treatment regimens. In terms of treatment outcomes, TP53-mutant patients exhibited significantly shorter mPFS compared with their wild-type counterparts (13.7 months, 95% CI, 8.3–19.2 vs. 18.8 months, 95% CI, 14.9–22.7; p = 0.006). Interestingly, the ORR did not differ significantly between the TP53-mutant and wild-type groups (57.1% [28/49] vs. 59.2% [42/71], p = 0.826).

Among the 49 patients with concurrent EGFR L858R and TP53 mutations, disease progression was observed in 40 cases (81.6%), with an mPFS of 13.7 months (95%CI, 8.3–19.2). At the time of data cutoff, 18 patients had succumbed to the disease. KM analysis demonstrated that patients with higher ECOG PS (=2) had higher risk of progression (HR, 2.554; 95%CI, 0.751–8.688) but not significant (Fig. 5a). Only pleural effusion was significantly associated with PFS (HR, 3.234; 95% CI, 1.292–8.096; p = 0.008) (Fig. 5b), and no clinical variables were found to be correlated with OS in this patient subgroup (Fig. 5c-d; Supp Table 1).
Discussion
Patients with EGFR L858R mutant NSCLC generally exhibit higher sensitivity to EGFR-TKI therapy among EGFR mutant types. However, a subset of patients developed early resistance and failed to achieve the expected therapeutic response [4]. Based on our analysis of EGFR-TKI efficacy in 120 patients with EGFR exon 21 L858R mutations, we identified several factors associated with worse clinical outcomes, including ECOG PS (=2), a higher number of metastatic organs (≥3), concurrent TP53 mutations, and lower BMI (≤24 kg/m2). These findings highlight the heterogeneity in treatment response among EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC patients and underscore the need for personalized therapeutic strategies.
In our study, ECOG PS was identified as an independent predictive factor for both PFS and OS in NSCLC patients with EGFR L858R mutation who received EGFR-TKIs at first-line treatment. This finding is consistent with existing literature, supporting ECOG PS as a widely used prognostic indicator in lung cancer [7], [18]. Our results further demonstrated that EGFR L858R-mutant patients with an ECOG PS of 2 experienced significantly shorter PFS and OS compared with those with better performance status. Simply, patients with higher ECOG PS could have an elevated risk when facing treatment-related adverse events, likely due to baseline comorbidities and functional decline.
We also noticed that patients with more metastatic organs or specific metastatic organs (liver or bone metastasis) exhibited worse responses to EGFR-TKI treatment. This observation aligns with the established understanding that metastatic spread in NSCLC is associated with adverse clinical outcomes [7], [19]. Notably, approximately 40% of NSCLC patients present with distant metastasis at the time of initial diagnosis [20], [21]. Among metastatic organs, liver metastasis appeared particularly detrimental, with affected patients facing an increased risk of mortality compared with those with other distant metastases [19], [22]. Similarly, bone metastasis has been associated with skeletal-related complications and a higher propensity for multi-organ metastases, including concurrent brain and liver involvement, which collectively contribute to poor prognosis in EGFR-mutant NSCLC [23]. In our cohort, the presence of increased tumor burden, as evidenced by multiple metastatic organs in EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC patients, emerged as an independent prognostic factor for OS, which is consistent with previous findings in patients with EGFR exon 19 del [8]. While the molecular mechanisms underlying this association are yet to be fully understood, the heterogeneous tumor microenvironment could play a role [24], influencing tumor biology, drug responsiveness, and disease progression.
Our findings also revealed that a higher BMI was associated with a preferable response to EGFR-TKIs in EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC patients. The role of obesity in diseases is arguable, which is widely recognized as a significant health concern linked to various chronic conditions, but associated with more favorable outcomes in obese individuals with certain diseases, including cancer [25], [26]. This "obesity paradox" has also been reported among cancer types. A meta-analysis showed that obesity was a protective factor for OS in gastrointestinal and lung cancer, but an adverse factor in breast cancers [27]. Its protective effect is further supported by studies showing that lung cancer patients with higher BMI levels have lower mortality rates than those with lower BMI [28], [29] and overweight (BMI > 24 kg/m2) EGFR mutant patients exhibited longer OS than normal-weight patients [30]. Nevertheless, the association between BMI and lung cancer outcomes remains controversial [31]. A previous study found no significant difference in PFS or OS between the obese and nonobese groups [32]. Similarly, Hisao et al. reported comparable efficacy of gefitinib in EGFR mutant NSCLC patients across BMI categories [33]. These conflicting findings underscored the prognostic significance of BMI in lung cancer. Further investigation could facilitate cancer management for NSCLC patients to achieve better outcomes in the future.
Previous studies demonstrated that TP53 mutations are the predominant co-occurring genomic alteration with EGFR mutations, with reported frequencies ranging from 30.9% to 41.4% [15], [34]. Our sequencing analysis revealed a TP53 co-mutation rate of 40.8% in EGFR L858R-mutant NSCLC patients. Importantly, we identified co-mutated TP53 as a significant predictor of reduced PFS in these patients, consistent with previous studies [35], [36]. Although the multivariate analysis in our study did not reach statistical significance, which could be due to the limited sample size, this emerging evidence underscores the critical role of co-occurring genomic alterations in shaping tumor heterogeneity and therapeutic responses. P53 as a well-known tumor suppressor, plays a crucial role in cancer suppression by regulating cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis in response to cellular stress and DNA damage. TP53 co-mutations contributing to EGFR-TKI resistance could be through induction of genomic instability and copy number variations [37]. While more comprehensive mechanisms require further investigation, the current findings regarding concurrent mutation have important therapeutic implications, providing a clue to combination therapeutic strategies of EGFR-TKIs and inhibitors to other mutations.
This study has several limitations. First, the relatively small sample size limit the statistical power of our findings. Second, the survival data were premature due to an insufficient follow-up duration. Third, the restricted scope of our gene mutation panel may have missed other clinically relevant genomic alterations that could impact treatment outcomes. Fourth, as a single-center retrospective study, potential selection bias and confounding factors may have affected the results. To address these limitations, we propose the following future directions: 1) conducting a multicenter, prospective study with a larger sample size to validate our findings; 2) implementing extended follow-up periods to obtain more robust survival data; 3) incorporating NGS to comprehensively characterize the genomic landscape; and 4) developing predictive models to guide the selection between EGFR-TKI monotherapy and combination strategies.
Conclusion
In this study, we demonstrated that the extensive metastatic burden (more metastic organs), concurrent TP53 mutations, worse ECOG PS, and reduced BMI were predictive of the response to EGFR-TKIs in NSCLC patients harboring EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation. These findings may provide clinicians with valuable prognostic indicators to optimize treatment strategies. Further validation through multicenter studies with larger cohorts is needed to confirm the clinical significance of these factors.
